activity.title: 🎄Christmas in July (the Network Engineers version, not the Hallmark version) Since late last year I've been strugging with a decision. Having already determined that understanding LLMs and the "AI" ecosystem would be essential to my work, I knew I needed local AI mostly for privacy but eventually also for cost. The words of Mitko Vasilev have been haunting me: "Make sure you own your AI. AI in the cloud is not aligned with you; it’s aligned with the company that owns it." Thats not to say I don't use Claude/ Claude Code , ChatGPT , Perplexity , Devin/Windsurf etc. on a daily basis and converted to Perplexity's Comet Browser almost exclusively for web searching a year ago. Those AI harnesses have their place but for me to really see what this new technology could do I needed private AI (on-prem LLM). So, do I get a new MAC with more unified memory? Do I build my own system? What to do... So one Saturday last month I headed to Central Computers in San Mateo to check out the offerings. - I didn't want another MAC (for this) - I wanted more familiarity with the NVIDIA ecosystem as that relates directly to what some of our clients are working on - I wanted something I could "cluster" if at all possible ... so I came home with one of the NVIDIA DGX Spark variants (mine from GIGABYTE ). I won't sugar coat it, the commercial Agent harnesses in general give you some great turnkey features. With local LLM power comes lots of Agent harness assembly. I didn't build a physical system but make no mistake, I built an Agent harness. This space is impoving daily (if not faster) and the exprience is well worth it if only for the bragging rights..."Yeah I remember when I had to make sure the model I used was trained for reliable tool calling.." ➡️ Quite a lengthy introduction to my Christmas in July story but introduction to what exactly? 📖 A *must* read! So grateful to Packt for sharing with me a pre release copy and asking me to review Sif Baksh 'n new book "Building AI Agents for Network Operations". If you invest in one book to understand what this is all about and how it plays into our network engineering discipline, THIS is it. Sif brings a wealth of well-grounded experience. 🎁🎁 For me it was a double gift: a pragmatic, relatively hype-free view of the current state, plus real-world examples to try. You don't need a DGX Spark to run them (though it's SO nice to worry less about resources). The models in the book are quite modest. But working the exercises on my Spark really jumpstarted my local LLM "assembly." As timely as it was for my Spark project, the book is much more. It maps the current landscape, what things are and are not, and positions the technology and tools in a very relatable way. It also helps place Network Automation alongside Agentic AI for those of us thinking, "What the heck... we were just getting our arms around automation, and now this?" I really hope you read this book! https://lnkd.in/gG6CaYkk

I’ve been reading about path dependence. In particular Paul A David 's "Clio and the Economics of QWERTY" (American Economic Review, 1985), written while he was in the Department of Economics at Stanford University which explains how early, accidental choices can lock us into suboptimal standards that persist because of network effects and sunk costs. Today’s network engineering feels a lot like that. We have decades of vendor lock‑in, CLI muscle memory, and legacy tooling entrenching us in a “QWERTY-era” for Network Design and Operations, even as automation and now agentic AI offer game changing value. If you’re ready to break out or want to continue breaking out of our industry’s path dependence, the Packet Coders team and Sif Baksh are offering a way forward: https://lnkd.in/gmPAtt5V

Erik Klaubert is the most talented Wireless Engineer I've ever worked with. Wireless is not my thing so I am lucky he is also incredibly patient as he explains things to me, like why so many of our recent projects are wireless focused (new APs, new design, upgraded switches which support newer PoE standards, new cabling). If you are also seeing a greater demand for an improved wireless experience for users and applications like AGVs (Automated Guided Vehicles), AMRs (Autonomous Mobile Robots), logistics automation systems (automated storage and retrieval, conveyor and sorting, and route‑optimized dispatch), and other mission‑critical industrial IoT workloads, I hope you find a few minutes to read Erik’s post https://lnkd.in/gNvPugZG

Network Automation Forum 's Autocon5 kicked off today with amazing content (again). Michael Bushong from Nokia started things off with his keynote "The Cognitive Biases Impacting Network Automation" or as I like to call it "Let me exploit how the human brain works so I can convince you Network Automation is good and that YOU need it!" ...and it just got better. I'm seeing the content in each presentation and across the AutoCon conferences become more mature and insightful, helping us all attack the problem from multiple sides. Lucas Immanuel Nickel - Network Operations Automation at DE-CIX "At this scale, NetOps automation needs SRE practices: reliable delivery, observability, and safe failures" Leo Fleskes & Gerasimos Tzakis - Modernizing Workflows as old as the Railways "Lessons Learned: Management buy-in, Blamess culture, Shared responsibility, Focus on MVP, Automation-friendly architecture" <--- pure gold Tim Sando - Meeting Automation in the Middle: Why NetOps Automation Can’t Wait "Automating verification mattered more than automating the shortcut". <---this does not get mentioned enough! Christian Adell & David Flores - Rethinking Network Monitoring "THE BETTER YOU DO THIS, THE MORE DATA YOU MAKE". <--- invaluable insight from those doing it There was so much more but these really hit home for me. If you are not here, keep your eye out for Ethan Banks , Drew Conry-Murray , and the Packet Pushers team for a far more thorough report. It is hard to describe how tempting it is to sneak out of my own presentation to go listen to Ivan Pepelnjak and others in the General Session tomorrow. Would that be be bad? Thankfully these will all be available on the NAF YouTube channel.

Network Automation Forum 's AutoCon5 starts tomorrow in Munich with workshops designed to help people move from thinking about network automation to actually doing it. A highlight is the purpose-built Foundational Workshop Track curated by Rick Donato and Gary Woodward of Packet Coders . The four-part series covers: 🐍 Python and structured data ⚙️ Configuration management with Git, Nornir, NAPALM, and Jinja2 ✅ Testing and validation with Pytest and APIs 🔄 CI/CD workflows with GitHub Actions These workshops go hand in hand with another AC5 first: the dedicated NAF Framework Track, where we will show the framework in action. The NAF Framework can help organizations: • Understand where to begin • Identify gaps in their current automation approach • Improve existing workflows • Evaluate tools based on the capabilities they provide • Build solutions without becoming locked into a specific vendor or platform What better way to illustrate that relationship than to map the foundational workshops directly to the NAF Framework? - Python and structured data provide a foundation across the framework. - Configuration management connects intent, orchestration, and execution. - Testing and validation span intent, observability, collection, and execution. - CI/CD brings those capabilities together into a repeatable, governed operational orchestrated workflow. NAF’s commitment to helping organizations get started with automation, regardless of their infrastructure vendors, is visible in every facet of the AutoCon conferences: the dedicated framework track, the curated foundational workshops, the technical sessions, and the people willing to share what they have learned. This feels less like a traditional conference and more like a community gathering of friends committed to sharing and improving as network operators and leaders. I can’t wait to see everyone in Munich! And for those who cannot join us: - keep an eye out for the Packet Pushers updates (you will miss the 1:1 and 1:many nerd interactions but Ethan Banks and his team will keep you updated on the highlights and then some) - start planning your trip this fall to AutoCon6 in North America (The location will be announced at the conclusion of AC5 ... as is tradition) #AutoCon5 #NetworkAutomation #NAFFramework #PacketCoders #Python #NetDevOps #CICD #NetworkEngineering #Automation

When I saw that the latest version of SuzieQ Enterprise supported MCP 🥳, I knew I had to take it through its paces. Dinesh Dutt and the Stardust Systems team are very deliberate about what they support, always focusing on useful features and on reducing tool feature "bloat", so if they added support for MCP it was time to take a look. I went all in. 📍 OpsMill Infrahub for intent 📍 SuzieQ for current state and validation 📍 Netmiko MCP server from Nuno Antunes for configuration updates 📍 Anthropic 's Claude Code 📍 Wispr Flow to talk to Claude I hope you find the information in the article useful and the LLM responses amusing! No need to worry...this is Sam Kinison-Lite https://lnkd.in/gY_g34jr

SuzieQ Enterprise quietly keeps making the product more powerful and easier to use with every update. Latest on this hit parade is an MCP server for SuzieQ from Stardust systems. In one Claude Code session, I had my assistant, Sam Kinison : 🧨 Audit VLANs at a location 🧨 Discover IP Phones 🧨 Decide whether VLAN 200 was a safe choice for a new office‑occupancy IoT segment at HQ 🧨 Then, via the Netmiko MCP server from Nuno Antunes , delete VLAN 200 on one switch, create it on another, and update the uplink trunk 🧨 Validate using Spanning Tree ... all from natural‑language prompts. In the same session, 🧨 I said I was a “new hire,” and asked for a description of the topology, devices, software versions, and configurations of HQ. Impressed 🤩 and slightly terrified 😱 in equal measure, this "out‑take" is just a teaser for a longer article I’m writing on MCP (what is it and where it fits) and how SuzieQ Enterprise MCP and an LLM make it effortless to interrogate your network (past, present, and occasionally future) while providing possibly unexpected insights. Network Automation Forum 's first AutoCon, AutoCon0, reasied a spirited debate on the "death of the CLI". With SuzieQ in the environment, we've pretty much stopped logging in to switches for state and configuration data because its easier to just query SuzieQ. Log in in the morning and keep the session up all day. No more hopping around logging in to a handfull of switches to figure something out. This additional layer of abstraction has opened up our ability to answer questions about the network to a far wider set of individuals, including the users. You no longer need switch access or knowledge of command syntax to get your questions answered. With the SuzieQ Enterprise MCP server the barrier to entry is now ZERO and may well deal a lasting body blow to the CLI. Now I can just ask: "What vlan is configured on interface G1/0/16 on the sea of cortez switch?" "Are there any issues with spanning tree at the LAX campus?" ... and if Im a little fuzzy on STP I can ask my LLM and get a tailored explanation using my network! ❯ I don't understand how spanning tree works. ❯OHHHH ROOKIE!! THIS IS WHERE WE BUILD YOU UP!! AAAHHH! Sit down ❯— we're gonna walk through STP using YOUR network at HQ so it sticks!! ❯ Spanning Tree Protocol — From Zero, With UWACO Examples I’ve been consistently urging caution when it comes to using LLMs in network operations. That said, in a read-only environment, the productivity gains and potential improvements in customer satisfaction are becoming hard to ignore. In many ways, this feels similar to the early days of network automation, when we started with pulling show commands. A useful, low-risk, activity and a stepping stone toward broader diciplined adoption. I hope my giggling all over the place at Sam's responses is not too distracting! https://lnkd.in/gCvcmJ_m #mcp #suzieq

activity.title: Packt offered me a chance to review 'Building AI Agents for Network Operations: Design LLM-powered NetOps workflows with Python, Ollama, MCP, and tool calling', by Sif Baksh . I already respect and admire Sif, his dedication, his skills and the way he approaches knowledge and how he shares it with the rest of us. This book however managed to surpass my expectations. I am not doing anyone a favor here when I say that I really think this book will serve as a ladder for me: it's the step I have been missing to get to the next level of my approach on how to really understand and use AI agents in my projects, using local models and how to connect them to my tooling and platforms with MCP. I am thrilled with what I have read so far, this is exactly what I needed. I intend to dig into this book for the rest of the summer and along with some additional training I have lined up, come out a better equipped engineer on the other end. If you were looking for a way into this, this is your chance. Highly recommended! The book is available on Amazon, here: https://lnkd.in/dQhDycNF

A 744-billion-parameter model now runs in my office. Four NVIDIA DGX Sparks. 100-gigabit RoCE fabric. GLM-5.2 at 4-bit, tensor-parallel across all four, 200,000-token context. 97.97 Gb/s node-to-node RDMA — 98% of line rate, first bring-up. Cold start to serving: 4 minutes 49 seconds. Zero restarts since launch. It reads a 160,000-token document in four minutes, and nothing leaves the building. Time to party, and by that I mean cable management. [UPDATE] This is messy, clearly, and 1 minute after setting it up to see if it even worked. Bolting it all down and securing it before knowing if you are missing something is dumb and creates more work. So if the only thing you have to comment on is that, show me your pristine setup, otherwise you are a talker not a builder.
